transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?
I’m here because after I eat too much, I make myself throw up so I won’t gain weight. It’s getting to the point where I’m scared I can’t stop doing it.
When you say you eat too much, do you consume an unusually large amount of food in a short period of time?

Yes. Usually late at night, after everyone’s quiet, I’ll just stand in the kitchen and keep eating—leftovers, cereal, chips, ice cream, whatever’s there. It goes way past a normal meal. Sometimes it looks like half the pantry has been picked over.
Could you tell me your current height and weight?
I’m not sure of my exact weight right now. I’m about average height, I think, but I haven’t measured myself recently.
What was your weight the last time you weighed yourself?
I honestly can’t remember. It’s been a while since I weighed myself, and I’ve been avoiding the scale.
Have your doctors or family members expressed concern that you are underweight or too thin?
No, not that I know of. Nobody’s said I look too thin or that I’m underweight.
On average, how many times a week do these episodes of overeating and making yourself throw up happen?
At least once most weeks for the past three months. Some weeks it’s several times, especially when I’m home more because of my back.
How much does your body shape or weight influence how you feel about yourself as a person?

A lot, honestly. If my work pants feel tight or I see my belly in the mirror, I feel like I’m failing at everything. Like I’m not the strong woman I used to be—the one who could handle transmissions and keep up with the guys.

latest_inference.note: Patient clearly satisfies all core criteria for Bulimia Nervosa (F50.2), including recurrent objective binge eating, compensatory purging (self-induced vomiting) occurring at least weekly for 3 months, undue influence of weight/shape on self-worth, and absence of low body weight. Atypical bulimia nervosa (F50.3) is ruled out.
